case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Medicare’s Disproportionate Share Hospital (DSH) formula counts a patient as “entitled to supplementary security income (SSI) benefits” based on SSI eligibility/status codes generally, or only if the patient was actually entitled to receive SSI cash payments during the month of the hospital stay.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 42 U.S.C. § 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I) (Medicare DSH “SSI fraction” referring to patients “entitled to supplementary security income benefits … under [Title] XVI”); cross-referenced Title XVI SSI provisions in 42 U.S.C. § 1381 et seq.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Hospitals argue that the statutory phrase “entitled to supplementary security income benefits” should be read broadly to include patients whom SSA data indicates were SSI-eligible or SSI-entitled in a status sense, even if SSA did not actually pay SSI cash benefits for the hospitalization month. They contend HHS improperly narrows the SSI fraction by treating “entitled” as requiring contemporaneous payment-entitlement, and that this interpretation undercounts low-income patients and reduces DSH payments, contrary to the DSH program’s purpose and to how SSA codes reflect entitlement.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Secretary argues “entitled to supplementary security income benefits” means entitled to receive SSI income-supplementing payments for the relevant month, not merely associated with SSI in SSA’s data codes. HHS’s approach aligns with the text (benefits under Title XVI are cash payments), the temporal link in the DSH fraction (entitlement while the patient received hospital services), and avoids sweeping in many people who are not SSI-eligible or are coded as ineligible/no-longer-eligible. The government also argues that differences between Medicare and SSI statutory schemes justify different uses of similar terms and that the hospitals’ reading would include many individuals not actually entitled to SSI payments.
key_precedents: Metropolitan Hospital v. HHS, 712 F.3d 248 (D.C. Cir. 2013)
Florida Health Sciences Center, Inc. v. Becerra, No. 19-cv-3487-RC, 2021 WL 2823104 (D.D.C. July 7, 2021)
Environmental Defense v. Duke Energy Corp., 549 U.S. 561 (2007)
Allina Health System v. Sebelius, 982 F. Supp. 2d 1 (D.D.C. 2013)

John Roberts.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point is that “entitled” can be a broader, status-based concept in Medicare (they will lean on Empire Health), but Justice Barrett is right that Empire was Medicare-Part-A specific and expressly did not decide the SSI-fraction question. Here the statute’s object—“supplementary security income benefits … under subchapter XVI”—and the temporal linkage (“for such days”) fit Title XVI’s month-by-month cash-payment entitlement, not untethered SSA status codes that may reflect suspension, termination, or ineligibility. Justice Kagan’s administrability concern reinforces the textual point: importing a thicket of codes would effectively rewrite Congress’s proxy and destabilize a technical reimbursement scheme. Duke Energy (raised by Justice Alito) further supports reading the same word in its statutory setting rather than forcing a Medicare term-of-art onto a cross-referenced Title XVI payment regime, so I would uphold the Secretary on narrow grounds without announcing a trans-substantive definition of “entitled.”

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point is that “entitled” can sometimes denote a broader program-status concept, and they invoke Empire Health to press that reading here. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, this provision cross-references Title XVI and speaks of “supplementary security income benefits,” which in that scheme are month-by-month cash payments; reading “entitled” to sweep in suspension/nonpay status codes would detach the statute’s temporal hook (“for such days”) from any legal right to benefits for the relevant month. Justice Alito’s citation to Environmental Defense v. Duke Energy reinforces that identical words may take their meaning from context, so Empire’s Medicare-Part-A gloss cannot be mechanically imported to override Title XVI’s payment-centered structure. Under an original public-meaning approach, the best reading remains that “entitled to … benefits” requires a present legal right to the SSI payment for that month, not an administrative classification that may reflect ineligibility or nonpay.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The hospitals’ best point remains that “entitled” can sometimes denote status rather than contemporaneous payment, and they invoke Empire Health to argue for a broad Medicare-wide gloss. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, this clause does not speak in Medicare Part A terms; it asks whether a patient was “entitled to supplementary security income benefits … under subchapter XVI” “for such days,” which naturally tracks Title XVI’s month-specific cash-payment entitlement, not SSA coding artifacts that may reflect suspension or nonpayability. Justice Kagan’s administrability concern reinforces the textual reading: importing a thicket of status codes would expand the numerator beyond those legally entitled to SSI benefits for the hospitalization month and destabilize a technical reimbursement regime. Environmental Defense v. Duke Energy, noted by multiple colleagues, confirms that Empire’s Medicare-specific usage does not control where Congress cross-references a distinct benefits scheme with different structural cues.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The petitioners’ best point remains that Congress likely used SSI as a low-income proxy and that broader SSA eligibility/status codes might capture similarly poor patients whose payments fluctuate, but that policy impulse cannot override the statute’s insistence on being “entitled to supplementary security income benefits … under subchapter XVI” “for such days,” which aligns with Title XVI’s month-specific cash-payment entitlement. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on the temporal hook and cross-reference persuades me that importing untethered SSA codes would dilute the statute’s focus and sweep in suspension/termination/nonpay categories that are not legal entitlement to SSI benefits for the hospitalization month. Justice Barrett’s discussion of Empire Health Foundation and the point (echoed by Justice Kagan and Justice Alito) that Duke Energy allows context-specific meanings undercuts the hospitals’ claim that Medicare’s broader “entitled” usage must control here. On pragmatic grounds tied to access and fairness, the Secretary’s approach also better constrains discretion and avoids making safety-net funding turn on opaque coding conventions rather than the actual legal right Congress referenced.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The petitioners’ best point remains that “entitled” can operate as a broader eligibility/status concept and that SSI is a proxy for low income, so we should not let month-to-month payment mechanics defeat the proxy. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett stress, the statute’s object is “supplementary security income benefits … under subchapter XVI” and it asks about entitlement “for such days,” which fits Title XVI’s month-specific legal right to a cash payment, not an SSA coding category that may include suspension, termination, or ineligibility. Justice Alito’s citation to Environmental Defense v. Duke Energy strengthens the contextual reading: Empire Health’s Medicare Part A usage does not control a cross-reference to a distinct benefits scheme with its own entitlement structure. On a pragmatic textualist view, the Secretary’s interpretation is both the better textual fit and the more administrable, statute-tethered rule in a technical reimbursement regime, so nothing in conference undermines my current position.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The hospitals’ best counter is that “entitled” can denote program status rather than payment, invoking Empire Health, but that overlooks that this provision asks whether the patient was “entitled to supplementary security income benefits … under title XVI” for the relevant days/month—where “benefits” are month-by-month cash payments and entitlement is correspondingly time-bound. Justice Barrett’s point remains decisive: Empire construed Medicare Part A within Medicare’s own scheme and expressly did not resolve the SSI cross-reference, so it cannot justify importing a Medicare term-of-art to override Title XVI’s payment-centered structure. Environmental Defense v. Duke Energy (noted by Justice Alito) reinforces that identical words may take their meaning from statutory context, and here the cross-referenced context is Title XVI, not SSA’s administratively convenient but overinclusive status codes. Justice Kagan’s administrability concern further supports the textual reading because the petitioners’ approach would sweep in suspension/termination/nonpay categories and thereby expand the numerator beyond what Congress authorized.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point remains that “entitled to” can sometimes denote broader statutory eligibility, and they will invoke Empire Health to press for a Medicare-wide, status-based reading. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett stress, the statutory object here is “supplementary security income benefits … under [Title] XVI,” where “benefits” are month-by-month cash payments, and the DSH fraction’s “for such days” linkage makes contemporaneous payment entitlement the most natural fit. Justice Kagan’s administrability point reinforces—not replaces—the text: relying on opaque SSA status codes that include suspension/termination/nonpay categories would expand the numerator beyond legal entitlement to Title XVI benefits for the hospitalization month and destabilize this technical reimbursement program. Environmental Defense v. Duke Energy, raised by several colleagues, confirms that we should not impose a uniform gloss on “entitled” across distinct statutory contexts, so Empire Health’s Medicare-specific construction does not control this cross-reference to Title XVI.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The petitioners’ strongest argument—that “entitled” in Medicare can be a broad status concept (invoking Empire Health)—does not overcome the text here, which asks whether the patient was “entitled to supplementary security income benefits … under subchapter XVI” and ties that inquiry to the hospitalization period (“for such days”), naturally tracking month-specific legal entitlement to Title XVI cash payments rather than SSA status codes that may include nonpayable or ineligible categories. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on the temporal hook reinforces that reading: a code untethered to a given month cannot sensibly answer whether one was entitled to benefits for that month’s inpatient days. Justice Kagan’s administrability point also cuts against petitioners because adopting a broad code-based numerator would expand the fraction beyond what Congress measured and make reimbursement turn on opaque coding conventions rather than Title XVI’s entitlement rules. Environmental Defense v. Duke Energy, noted by Justices Alito and Gorsuch, further supports giving “entitled” a context-sensitive meaning tied to the cross-referenced SSI scheme, so Empire’s Medicare-specific gloss does not control.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The hospitals’ strongest point remains that “entitled” in Medicare can be status-based (they lean on Empire Health), but Justice Barrett and the Chief Justice persuasively explain why that Medicare-specific gloss cannot be transplanted onto a clause that expressly ties entitlement to Title XVI “benefits” and to the hospitalization days (“for such days”). Justice Alito’s and Justice Kagan’s reliance on Environmental Defense v. Duke Energy reinforces a context-sensitive reading: identical words can mean different things across statutory schemes, and here Title XVI’s month-by-month cash-benefit structure supplies the relevant content. From a procedural-fairness and consequences-focused perspective, using actual month-specific entitlement to SSI cash benefits better constrains agency discretion and avoids making hospital reimbursement turn on opaque or overinclusive SSA status codes that may reflect suspension, termination, or ineligibility rather than a legal right to payment during the hospitalization period.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Medicare DSH statute asks whether a patient was “entitled to [SSI] benefits … under subchapter XVI” in the period “for such days” the patient received inpatient services, 42 U.S.C. § 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I), which naturally links the inquiry to a contemporaneous legal right to SSI cash payments for that month, not to broader SSA status/eligibility codes untethered from payment entitlement. Title XVI’s “benefits” are income-supplementing cash payments, so reading “entitled” to mean entitled-to-be-paid fits the statutory text and avoids importing administrative coding artifacts into a reimbursement formula. Consistent with Environmental Defense v. Duke Energy Corp., 549 U.S. 561 (2007), identical words can bear different meanings in different statutory settings; thus hospitals’ appeal to a Medicare-wide “entitled” gloss does not overcome the DSH provision’s temporal and substantive focus. A narrow ruling upholding the Secretary’s month-of-service payment-entitlement approach best respects Congress’s chosen words and preserves institutional stability in a complex reimbursement regime without rewriting the fraction by judicially expanding who counts as “entitled.”

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text asks whether a patient was “entitled to supplementary security income benefits … under [Title] XVI” during the period the patient “was furnished” inpatient hospital services. 42 U.S.C. § 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I). At enactment and in Title XVI’s ordinary usage, “SSI benefits” principally denotes the monthly cash payment authorized under 42 U.S.C. § 1382, so “entitled” most naturally refers to a present legal right to that payment for the relevant month, not merely an administrative status code or historical association in SSA data. Reading “entitled” to include non-payable or ineligible coded statuses would sever the statute’s temporal link and expand the fraction beyond what the words can bear, and I would not rewrite the statute to serve perceived programmatic purposes. Cf. Environmental Defense v. Duke Energy Corp., 549 U.S. 561 (2007) (same term may take meaning from statutory context), supporting the Secretary’s context-specific reading.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text asks whether the patient was “entitled to supplementary security income benefits … under [Title] XVI” “for such month” in which the patient received the inpatient hospital services, 42 U.S.C. § 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I), and under Title XVI the relevant “benefits” are the monthly cash payments SSI provides—not merely an administrative status code untethered to payment entitlement. Reading “entitled” to mean actually entitled to receive SSI cash payments for the hospitalization month best fits that temporal linkage and avoids sweeping in individuals coded in SSA data as ineligible, suspended, or otherwise not entitled to payment, with significant practical and fiscal consequences for the DSH program. Although Becerra v. Empire Health Foundation, 597 U.S. 424 (2022), construed “entitled to [Medicare Part A] benefits” broadly, Environmental Defense v. Duke Energy Corp., 549 U.S. 561 (2007), cautions that identical words can take different meanings in different statutory contexts; here the cross-reference to Title XVI and the month-specific inquiry support the Secretary’s narrower, payment-focused reading. The Secretary’s interpretation therefore better adheres to the statutory text and administrability, while respecting Congress’s chosen metrics rather than expanding the fraction based on imperfect coding conventions.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The SSI fraction counts patients “entitled to supplementary security income benefits … under [Title] XVI” during the period they “received” inpatient services, 42 U.S.C. § 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I), and under Title XVI “benefits” are monthly cash payments payable only if the person is determined eligible for that month (see 42 U.S.C. §§ 1381a, 1382(c)(1)). Reading “entitled” to mean mere status codes untethered to actual monthly payment entitlement would sweep in individuals not eligible for a cash payment for the hospitalization month, diluting the statutory link to low-income patients and inviting error from administrative coding conventions not incorporated into Medicare by Congress. While Empire Health Foundation v. Becerra interprets “entitled to” Part A broadly as program qualification, it also underscores that the meaning of “benefits” depends on the entitlement program at issue, and SSI’s entitlement is inherently month-and-payment specific. Consistent with Environmental Defense v. Duke Energy, similar words can take different content when the statutory programs differ, and nothing in § 1395ww directs HHS to treat SSA status codes as dispositive over Title XVI’s payment-based entitlement rules.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Medicare DSH SSI fraction asks whether a patient was “entitled to supplementary security income benefits … under subchapter XVI” “for such days,” 42 U.S.C. § 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I), which naturally points to entitlement to the Title XVI “benefits” that SSI actually provides—cash payment eligibility for the relevant month of inpatient service—rather than any broader administrative status code. Reading “entitled … benefits” to require contemporaneous payment-entitlement also best fits the provision’s day-linked fraction and avoids sweeping in many codes that denote ineligibility or termination, a workability concern reflected in Metro. Hosp. v. HHS, 712 F.3d 248, 268 (D.C. Cir. 2013), and Fla. Health Scis. Ctr., Inc. v. Becerra, 2021 WL 2823104, at *1. And under Environmental Defense v. Duke Energy Corp., 549 U.S. 561, 574 (2007), even identical terms can legitimately vary with statutory context, so any asserted cross-scheme inconsistency in how “entitled” is used does not defeat the Secretary’s context-sensitive reading.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I) asks whether the patient was “entitled to supplementary security income benefits … under [Title] XVI” for the month the patient “was entitled to benefits under part A,” tying the SSI inquiry to contemporaneous entitlement to Title XVI “benefits,” i.e., SSI cash payments, not merely a status code in SSA data. Reading “benefits” as actual payment-entitlement fits the ordinary meaning and Title XVI’s structure, and avoids expanding the fraction by administrative labels that can include ineligible or nonpay cases, a result the text does not authorize. Purpose-driven arguments cannot displace the statute’s plain terms, and differences in statutory schemes allow the same word to operate with scheme-specific meaning, consistent with Environmental Defense v. Duke Energy Corp., 549 U.S. 561 (2007). Auburn Regional describes the SSI fraction as measuring low-income Medicare patients “as measured by their entitlement to SSI benefits,” reinforcing a payment-entitlement understanding rather than a broader coding-based proxy.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The best reading of 42 U.S.C. § 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I) ties “entitled to supplementary security income benefits … under [Title] XVI” to entitlement to receive SSI’s Title XVI cash payments for the relevant month, because Title XVI defines SSI “benefits” as income-supplementing cash assistance and the DSH fraction is explicitly month-specific (counting patients “for such days” they received hospital services). That interpretation also fits the statute’s practical administration and avoids importing broad SSA status codes that may include individuals not actually eligible for SSI cash payment in that month. Consistent with Environmental Defense v. Duke Energy Corp., the same word can take meaning from context, and Metropolitan Hospital v. HHS supports treating “entitled” in the SSI portion as tethered to SSI’s cash-payment structure rather than a generalized status label. Respecting that contextual, workable construction aligns with precedent and institutional restraint in a technically complex Medicare payment scheme.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Medicare DSH provision asks whether, “for such days,” the patient “was entitled to supplementary security income benefits … under title XVI,” 42 U.S.C. § 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I), and under Title XVI the “benefits” Congress provides are cash payments designed to “assure a minimum level of income.” Reading “entitled to … benefits” in its ordinary textual sense thus ties entitlement to a legal right to receive an SSI payment for the relevant month, not to the presence of an SSA eligibility/status code that may reflect nonpayment or ineligibility. While Empire Health Foundation v. Becerra construed “entitled to benefits under Part A” broadly, it expressly reserved the SSI question and relied on Medicare-specific usage; importing that Medicare term-of-art into Title XVI ignores statutory context and the cross-referenced SSI scheme. Given that context and the temporal linkage (“for such days”) in § 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I), the Secretary’s payment-entitlement approach best fits the text and avoids counting individuals not actually entitled to SSI payments during the hospitalization month.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Medicare DSH SSI fraction asks whether the patient was “entitled to supplementary security income benefits … under [Title] XVI” “for such days” of hospitalization, 42 U.S.C. § 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I), which naturally ties the inquiry to contemporaneous eligibility for Title XVI cash-benefit payments rather than broader SSA status/administrative codes that may reflect ineligibility or nonpayment. Treating “entitled” as satisfied by status codes that include many “not eligible/no longer eligible” categories risks diluting the accuracy of the low-income proxy and produces practical consequences (over- or under-inclusion) unmoored from the statute’s temporal focus on the hospitalization month. Environmental Defense v. Duke Energy supports the Secretary’s argument that the shared word “entitled” can reasonably take on different operational meaning when linked to different statutory objects and implementation strategies, especially where Medicare is using SSI as an external proxy rather than administering SSI itself. Consistent with Metropolitan Hospital and Florida Health Sciences Center, I would uphold HHS’s interpretation as the better fit with the text, structure, and administrability of the DSH calculation while preserving procedural regularity in how agencies translate cross-program references into workable rules.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Medicare’s Disproportionate Share Hospital (DSH) calculation must treat patients as “entitled to supplementary security income (SSI) benefits” based on certain Social Security Administration (SSA) status codes even when those patients were not actually eligible for, or receiving, SSI cash payments during the hospital stay.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 42 U.S.C. § 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I) (Medicare DSH fraction—reference to patients “entitled to supplementary security income benefits ... under [Title] XVI”); Title XVI of the Social Security Act, 42 U.S.C. § 1381 et seq. (SSI benefits framework).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Hospitals argue that the statutory phrase “entitled to supplementary security income benefits” should be read broadly to include patients identified by various SSA SSI-related payment/status codes (including codes reflecting suspended, terminated, or otherwise non-pay statuses), because those codes indicate an SSI entitlement relationship sufficient for the Medicare DSH proxy. They contend the Secretary’s narrower approach—counting essentially only those actually entitled to SSI cash payments during the inpatient period—improperly excludes many low-income patients Congress meant DSH to capture, depresses DSH payments, and inconsistently treats “entitled” across related benefit contexts.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Secretary argues that in this Medicare provision “entitled to SSI benefits” refers to patients who, at the time they received hospital services, were entitled to SSI income-supplementing payments under Title XVI (i.e., eligible for and payable SSI cash benefits), not merely associated with an SSI application/record or a non-pay status code. The government emphasizes that many of the status codes hospitals seek to include explicitly denote ineligibility or loss of eligibility, so counting them would sweep in people not entitled to SSI at all; it also maintains that any perceived intra-statutory inconsistency can be explained by different statutory contexts and that the agency’s interpretation aligns with the D.C. Circuit’s understanding of the Medicare/SSI linkage.

Environmental Defense v. Duke Energy Corp., 549 U.S. 561 (2007) (as referenced in the record excerpt)
Allina Health System v. Sebelius, 982 F. Supp. 2d 1 (D.D.C. 2013) (as referenced in the record excerpt)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—echoing Empire Health—that “entitled” cannot be collapsed into actual payment has force as a general matter, but it loses traction once Congress specifically tied this proxy to “supplementary security income benefits … under Title XVI,” a cash-benefit program in which many disputed status codes affirmatively denote suspension, termination, or ineligibility rather than mere payment routing. As Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, the temporal phrase “for such days” reinforces that the inquiry is contemporaneous entitlement to Title XVI benefits, not a broader low-income affiliation that persists through non-entitlement months. Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Duke Energy is persuasive here: the same word (“entitled”) can carry different content across Medicare subclauses, and Empire’s Part A context does not compel importing a broader concept of entitlement into a cross-reference that incorporates Title XVI’s own entitlement/payability rules. On narrow, institutional grounds, I would uphold the Secretary’s approach without opining on every edge case, holding only that codes reflecting suspension/termination/non-pay ineligibility are not “entitled … under Title XVI” for the relevant inpatient days.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best argument is that SSI is a low-income proxy and that Empire Health rejected treating “entitled” as requiring an “absolute right to payment.” But Empire construed Medicare Part A, where “entitlement” is a beneficiary-status concept that can persist even when Medicare is not the payer; as Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Congress here cross-referenced “supplementary security income benefits … under Title XVI,” a cash-benefit scheme in which many of the disputed codes denote suspension/termination or non-payability—i.e., no present legal right to the Title XVI benefit for the relevant period. The temporal phrase “for such days” further ties the Medicare numerator to contemporaneous Title XVI entitlement, not to broader administrative classifications untethered from payability. Under a textualist, original-public-meaning approach, statutory purpose cannot expand “entitled to … benefits under Title XVI” to include statuses Title XVI itself treats as non-entitlement for the days at issue.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that SSI operates as a low-income proxy and that Empire Health warns against equating “entitled” with actual payment, including where payment is withheld for administrative reasons. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Congress did not refer to “low income” in the abstract; it tethered the DSH numerator to being “entitled to supplementary security income benefits … under Title XVI,” and Title XVI “benefits” are the payable cash assistance—so status codes that denote suspension/termination/non-pay are difficult to reconcile with being “entitled … [to] benefits” for “such days.” Empire Health’s Medicare Part A context, where entitlement can persist despite nonpayment because of the coverage/beneficiary-status structure, does not translate cleanly to Title XVI’s payability-based regime, and adopting Sotomayor’s broader proxy-driven reading would sever the Medicare cross-reference from the incorporated SSI rules and distort the DSH adjustment in practice. The cited context principle (as Justice Kavanaugh notes via Duke Energy) reinforces that “entitled” can sensibly track different legal concepts across different statutory programs, and here the Secretary’s narrower, payability-linked line better fits the cross-reference and temporal language.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The opposing side’s strongest point, pressed by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan, is that Title XVI is a cash-benefits program and that “for such days” plus “SSI benefits” implies contemporaneous payability, making suspension/termination codes hard to count as “entitled.” But that reading still risks collapsing “entitled” into “paid,” even though SSI eligibility is determined on a monthly basis and payment can be withheld for administrative or procedural reasons that do not negate the underlying low-income status Congress used as a proxy in the DSH fraction. Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Duke Energy—that identical words can differ by context—cuts both ways: here the DSH formula’s proxy function is itself a contextual signal against importing an overly payment-mechanical rule that systematically undercounts indigent patients because of coding/payment artifacts. Empire Health does not control, but it reinforces that “entitled” need not mean an absolute, presently payable check; where the statute’s purpose is to measure treatment of the poor, I would not read the cross-reference to Title XVI to exclude economically vulnerable patients based on nonpayment statuses unless Congress spoke more clearly.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best argument is that SSI operates as a low-income proxy and that Empire Health warns against collapsing “entitled” into “paid,” but that precedent’s logic depends on Medicare Part A’s coverage-status structure, where entitlement can persist even when payment is not due for a particular stay. Here, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Congress cross-referenced “supplementary security income benefits … under Title XVI,” and in that cash-benefit regime many of the disputed SSA codes signify suspension/termination or other non-pay states—hard to reconcile with ordinary usage of being “entitled to … benefits” for “such days.” Environmental Defense v. Duke Energy (raised by Justice Kavanaugh) reinforces that symmetry across subclauses cannot override this context, so importing non-pay/ineligible codes would decouple the Medicare proxy from Title XVI’s own entitlement/payability rules and make the line less coherent and less workable. I therefore see no legal argument here that undermines the Secretary’s narrower, context-specific construction.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor presses the best point: SSI is a low-income proxy and Empire Health rejects treating “entitled” as synonymous with actual payment, so excluding suspended/nonpay months could undercount poor patients. But, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Empire’s analysis was tethered to Medicare Part A’s coverage-status architecture, where “entitlement” can persist even when Medicare is not the payer; here Congress instead cross-referenced “supplementary security income benefits … under Title XVI,” a cash-benefits regime in which many disputed codes denote suspension/termination or other nonpayability that negates any present legal right to the Title XVI “benefit” for the relevant period. The phrase “for such days” reinforces that the inquiry is temporal and contemporaneous—linking the Medicare fraction to Title XVI’s own month-specific entitlement/payability rules rather than a broader program-affiliation proxy. Duke Energy, noted by Justice Kavanaugh, supports this context-specific reading: identical words need not carry identical meanings across different statutory schemes, and nothing in the enacted text authorizes expanding “entitled … to benefits under Title XVI” to include statuses Title XVI itself treats as not eligible/payable for that period.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point remains that SSI status is a low-income proxy and that Empire Health cautions against reading “entitled” as synonymous with actual payment, but Empire involved Medicare Part A where entitlement can persist even when Medicare is not the payer for a particular stay. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Congress here cross-referenced “SSI benefits … under Title XVI” and added the temporal limiter “for such days,” which most naturally ties the inquiry to contemporaneous Title XVI eligibility/payability—not to SSA status codes that affirmatively denote suspension, termination, or ineligibility. Duke Energy (noted by Justice Kagan and consistent with my view) supports treating identical words differently across statutory contexts when structure and cross-references differ, and that context-specific reading also promotes administrable, stable lines in a nationwide reimbursement formula. Nothing raised in conference undermines the Secretary’s narrower construction sufficiently to justify overruling it absent clearer statutory direction.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that SSI is a low-income proxy and Empire Health cautions against collapsing “entitled” into “paid”—does not overcome the specific cross-reference Congress chose: “supplementary security income benefits … under Title XVI” for the relevant days. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, Title XVI “benefits” are cash payments conditioned on contemporaneous eligibility/payability, and many of the disputed status codes indicate suspension/termination/nonpay that negate any present legal right to those benefits for that period. Empire Health is therefore contextually distinguishable because Medicare Part A entitlement can persist even when Medicare is not the payer, while here importing nonpay/ineligible codes would sever the Medicare fraction from Title XVI’s own entitlement rules and erode the administrable, payment-linked line recognized in Metropolitan Hospital. Under an originalist/textualist approach, purpose as proxy cannot expand “entitled … under Title XVI” beyond what Title XVI itself makes one legally entitled to receive for those days.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is the equitable one: SSI is a low-income proxy, and counting only paid months may undercapture vulnerable patients when payments are withheld for administrative reasons. But as Justice Kagan and Chief Justice Roberts stress, Congress did not incorporate “SSI-like” poverty status; it keyed the numerator to being “entitled to supplementary security income benefits … under Title XVI” “for such days,” and many of the disputed codes denote suspension/termination/nonpay states that Title XVI itself treats as nonpayable—so including them would detach the Medicare proxy from the very entitlement/payability framework Congress cross-referenced. Empire Health meaningfully informs the word “entitled,” yet, as Justice Kavanaugh notes via Duke Energy, context matters: Medicare Part A can preserve entitlement despite nonpayment for a stay, while Title XVI cash benefits turn on contemporaneous payable eligibility, making a payment-linked, day-tethered rule more textually and administratively coherent. On pragmatic fairness grounds, I also remain concerned that a code-driven overinclusive numerator would produce arbitrary windfalls and uneven treatment across hospitals based on opaque SSA coding rather than legally operative entitlement for the inpatient days.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I) asks whether the patient was “entitled to supplementary security income benefits ... under [Title] XVI” at the time the inpatient services were furnished, and Title XVI entitlement is tied to eligibility for, and payable receipt of, SSI cash assistance—not merely the existence of an SSA record or a status code that may reflect suspension or termination. Unlike Becerra v. Empire Health Foundation (2022), where “entitled to benefits” under Medicare Part A functioned as a term of art for program qualification even when payment was limited, the SSI phrase here points to an income-support payment status that many of the hospitals’ proposed codes expressly denote is not payable or not eligible. Counting non-pay/ineligible codes would broaden the numerator beyond Congress’s chosen proxy and would risk administrability and institutional legitimacy by forcing Medicare to treat “entitled” as overriding Title XVI’s own eligibility rules. Consistent with Metropolitan Hospital v. HHS (D.C. Cir. 2013), I would uphold the Secretary’s narrower, context-specific reading on the narrow ground that these non-pay status codes do not establish Title XVI entitlement during the relevant hospital stay.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text asks whether a patient was “entitled to supplementary security income benefits … under [Title] XVI,” 42 U.S.C. § 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I), and Title XVI makes entitlement turn on meeting statutory eligibility conditions for, and being payable, SSI cash benefits for the relevant month—not merely possessing an SSA record or a status code reflecting suspension/termination or other non-pay conditions. Reading “entitled” to include codes that expressly denote ineligibility or non-pay status would depart from the ordinary public meaning of “entitled” as having a present legal right to the benefit and would sever the Medicare proxy from the SSI program Congress referenced. Although Empire Health construed “entitled to [Medicare Part A] benefits” broadly, that holding rested on Part A’s beneficiary status structure and does not justify importing SSA administrative coding conventions that capture non-entitlement into Title XVI’s distinct eligibility/payability framework. Under a textualist approach, the Secretary’s construction best matches the incorporated Title XVI criteria and avoids counting persons not legally entitled to SSI payments during the service period.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Medicare DSH statute asks whether a patient was “entitled to supplementary security income benefits … under [Title] XVI” during the relevant inpatient period, 42 U.S.C. § 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I), and “benefits” in Title XVI are income-supplementing cash payments payable only when the claimant is eligible and not in a suspended or terminated (non-pay) status. Treating SSA status codes that expressly reflect non-pay, suspension, or loss of eligibility as “entitled” would detach the term from its ordinary legal meaning and produce the practical consequence of inflating the SSI proxy with persons not actually qualifying for SSI payments at the time—something Congress could not have intended for this targeted adjustment. Becerra v. Empire Health Foundation, 597 U.S. 424 (2022), does not compel the hospitals’ broader reading because it construed “entitled to [Medicare Part A] benefits” in a different programmatic context where entitlement can exist despite nonpayment for a particular stay, whereas here the cited codes often denote absence of Title XVI entitlement itself. Given the statutory text and the risk of overinclusion undermining the DSH mechanism, I would uphold the Secretary’s narrower, payment-linked interpretation.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: In § 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I), Congress used SSI entitlement as a proxy for low-income status in the Medicare DSH fraction, and that purpose is best served by treating “entitled to supplementary security income benefits” as turning on SSI program eligibility rather than actual receipt of a cash payment during the inpatient stay. This Court in Becerra v. Empire Health Foundation rejected reading “entitled” as requiring an “absolute right” to payment, supporting a broader, eligibility-based understanding of entitlement in closely related Medicare contexts. Excluding patients flagged by SSA SSI-related status codes solely because payment was suspended/withheld risks systematically undercounting vulnerable low-income beneficiaries and undermining the remedial function of DSH, contrary to Congress’s design. Given the statute’s proxy function and Empire’s construction of “entitled,” the Secretary’s cash-payment-only approach reads “entitled” too narrowly in this setting.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Medicare DSH numerator asks whether patients were “entitled to supplementary security income benefits … under [Title] XVI,” 42 U.S.C. § 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I), and in ordinary benefits-law usage that phrasing points to current legal eligibility for, and payability of, Title XVI cash assistance—not merely the existence of an SSA record or a status code that may reflect suspension, termination, or other non-pay states. Reading “entitled … benefits” to include codes that denote ineligibility would stretch the text beyond its workable meaning and risk counting individuals who are not entitled to SSI at all, undermining statutory coherence in using SSI as a low-income proxy. Petitioners’ reliance on intra-subsection symmetry with the Part A phrase is weakened by context: this Court has recognized that identical words can bear different meanings in different statutory settings, Environmental Defense v. Duke Energy Corp., 549 U.S. 561 (2007), and the SSI cross-reference here specifically ties entitlement to Title XVI benefits. Given the technical administration of SSI eligibility and the need for a workable rule in a complex payment formula, the Secretary’s payability-focused interpretation is at least the better textual fit and merits deference to the extent ambiguity remains.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I) asks whether, “for such days,” patients were “entitled to supplementary security income benefits … under [Title] XVI,” and Title XVI’s “supplementary security income” is a cash payment due only for months of payable eligibility, not merely the existence of an SSA record or a non-pay status code. Reading “entitled to … benefits” to include suspended/terminated/non-pay statuses would detach the text from the benefit Congress referenced—an income-supplementing payment—and sweep in persons Title XVI deems not eligible to receive any payment for the relevant period. Becerra v. Empire Health Foundation, 597 U.S. 424 (2022), is not to the contrary: it construed “entitled to [Medicare Part A] benefits” in a program where entitlement denotes qualifying for Part A coverage even if Medicare is not the payer, whereas here Congress specified “SSI benefits … under Title XVI,” whose entitlement turns on payable cash eligibility for the month. Given the statute’s temporal focus (“for such days”) and the ordinary meaning of “benefits” in Title XVI, the Secretary’s interpretation best fits the enacted text without resort to expansive agency gloss.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Medicare DSH provision asks whether, “for such days,” a patient was “entitled to supplementary security income benefits … under [Title] XVI,” 42 U.S.C. § 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I), which most naturally refers to legal eligibility for payable SSI cash benefits during the relevant inpatient days—not merely the existence of an SSA record or a status code that may reflect suspension or termination. Counting status codes that expressly denote non-pay or ineligibility would stretch “entitled” beyond its ordinary meaning and undermine administrable, workable line-drawing for a nationwide payment formula, a practical consideration that favors the Secretary’s approach. Consistent with this Court’s recognition that identical words can take different meanings in different statutory contexts, Environmental Defense v. Duke Energy Corp., 549 U.S. 561 (2007), the SSI-reference here can reasonably be tied to actual Title XVI benefit entitlement during the hospital stay rather than broader program affiliation. And the D.C. Circuit’s reading in Metropolitan Hospital v. HHS, 712 F.3d 248 (D.C. Cir. 2013), supports the Secretary’s narrower construction in this specialized Medicare reimbursement setting, which counsels restraint in upsetting the settled administrative framework.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of 42 U.S.C. § 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I) counts days for patients “entitled to supplementary security income benefits … under [Title] XVI,” and in ordinary legal usage “entitled” denotes a present legal right to receive the benefit, not merely an administrative record or non-pay status code that may reflect suspension or termination. Reading “entitled” to include codes that “explicitly denote ineligibility or loss of eligibility” would detach the Medicare proxy from Title XVI’s actual benefit conferral and would expand the numerator beyond those Congress chose to identify by reference to SSI “benefits.” Metropolitan Hospital v. HHS, 712 F.3d 248, 268–69 (6th Cir. 2013), upheld the Secretary’s interpretation that entitlement to SSI in this fraction turns on current eligibility/payability, and it also recognized that any tension with Medicare Part A “entitlement” is explained by structural differences between the SSI and Medicare schemes. Given that precedent and the statutory cross-reference to Title XVI benefits, I would affirm the Secretary’s narrower, payment-linked construction rather than an approach driven by SSA status codes alone.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Medicare DSH statute counts patient days for those who (for such days) were “entitled to supplementary security income benefits” under Title XVI, 42 U.S.C. § 1395ww(d)(5)(F)(vi)(I), which most naturally ties entitlement to contemporaneous eligibility/payability of SSI cash assistance during the inpatient stay, not merely the existence of an SSA record or a non-pay status code. Many of the codes hospitals seek to include (e.g., suspension or termination codes) reflect ineligibility or non-pay status, and treating them as “entitled” would distort the proxy Congress chose and produce substantial, administratively unworkable overinclusion with significant fiscal consequences. Consistent with Environmental Defense v. Duke Energy Corp., 549 U.S. 561 (2007), the same word can take its meaning from context, and here the “for such days” language and the linkage to Title XVI’s cash-benefit framework support the Secretary’s narrower construction. This reading also accords with the D.C. Circuit’s understanding of the Medicare/SSI linkage in Metropolitan Hospital v. HHS, 712 F.3d 248 (D.C. Cir. 2013), reinforcing procedural regularity and administrable lines in a complex benefits program.
